title: Rabbi Aryeh Levin walked to the underground prisoners in jail every Shabbat, and they called him "Father of the Prisoners"

trailer.text: Rabbi Aryeh Leib Levin was a renowned Jerusalem Torah scholar and tzaddik, known mainly for his many acts of kindness.
During the British Mandate he went to visit Jewish prisoners in the prisons, among them the underground prisoners.
For 25 years he came to the prison every Shabbat and festival, in all weather, without pay.
He prayed with the prisoners in a room converted into a synagogue, and according to the museum he loved them as sons and they saw him as a father.
According to JTA, some 1,000 former prisoners of the British signed a scroll in his honor.

stations.title: A poor child from Orla, a man of two rooms

paragraphs.text: According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, Aryeh Levin was born in Orla, near Grodno, to poor parents.
According to the museum's biography, he knew poverty and want from childhood.
According to the Lehi website, he decided to immigrate to the Land of Israel, arrived in Jaffa in 1905 and there met Rabbi Kook.

According to the Lehi website, in the Hebrew year Tarsah, Rabbi Aryeh married Zipporah Hannah, daughter of Rabbi Shapiro of Kovno. According to the museum's biography, four of his 11 children died young.
During World War I his family nearly starved.
Even when the economic situation in the country improved, he continued to live in two meager rooms in a modest apartment in the Mishkenot Yisrael neighborhood.
He served as mashgiach at the Etz Chaim Talmud Torah in Jerusalem until his death.

stations.title: "Only the Jews have no one to look after them"

paragraphs.text: According to the museum's biography, in the early twenties the underground prisoners were few, and their number grew from the time of the Arab Revolt.
According to his grandson, Reb Aryeh heard that two young men from the Merkaz HaRav yeshiva had been imprisoned in the Russian Compound, and went to visit them.
There, the grandson said, he discovered that the Muslim prisoners had a qadi, the Christians had a priest, and only the Jews had no one to look after them.
According to Jewishmag, as early as 1927 he began visiting Jewish prisoners who had been convicted of political offenses, such as possessing a weapon or smuggling.
According to the museum's biography, the British had difficulty finding a rabbi who would come to the prison every Shabbat and festival and pray with the prisoners.
According to the museum, after an approach to the Chief Rabbinate, Rabbi Kook recommended him, and he agreed on one condition: that he would not receive pay.
According to the museum, Rabbi Kook said that dealing with criminals requires largeness of heart, patience and love of kindness, and that Reb Aryeh was therefore suited.
According to the museum, one of the Jerusalem zealots insulted him in public because of his closeness to Rabbi Kook, and he restrained himself.

According to the museum's biography, Reb Aryeh greatly esteemed the underground prisoners, especially the members of the Irgun and Lehi, because they were persecuted by the British and held a minority view in the Yishuv.

stations.title: Every Shabbat and festival, in all weather

paragraphs.text: For 25 years the rabbi came to the prison every Shabbat and festival, in all weather, without pay or salary.
In the forties, the meeting with him was held inside the prison, in a room that had been converted into a synagogue.
Prisoners who were not religious also came to the Shabbat prayers, because their hearts were captivated by his goodness of heart and his righteousness.
According to his grandson, the Jewish prisoners, both Haredi and anti-religious, came to the prayers in his honor.
According to the museum's biography, he loved the prisoners as sons, and they returned his love and saw him as a father.
According to the museum, thanks to his fatherly attitude he reformed many hardened criminals.
Geula Cohen, a Lehi prisoner, said that he did not take them out from between the walls, but brought freedom in to them between the walls.

stations.title: From the cell to the families' homes

paragraphs.text: Even after Shabbat ended, the rabbi did not return home until he had visited the worried families and passed on greetings from their loved ones.
According to the Lehi website, the British did not know that he was passing letters between the prisoners and their families and members of the underground who were free.
Thanks to his energetic efforts, a kosher kitchen was set up in the prison.
According to the Lehi website, as the number of Jewish political prisoners grew, he began a struggle to separate them from the Arab prisoners.
According to the museum, the rabbi also visited the women's prison in Bethlehem several times.
According to his grandson, Shulamit Shamir went on a hunger strike in the women's prison in Bethlehem in order to see her son.
Her family turned to Reb Aryeh, he spoke with her, and she ended the hunger strike, the grandson said.
According to the museum, when he visited the patients at the leper hospital in Talbiyeh, they told him it was the first time anyone had visited them.

stations.title: The Shabbat on which the prisoners donated from their lives

paragraphs.text: According to Jewishmag, one Shabbat, while he was reading the Torah with the prisoners, he was called outside, and his son-in-law was waiting for him at the prison gate. They walked to the Shaarei Chesed neighbourhood, where his married daughter lived, and there he learned that she had been paralysed.
According to the museum, on the following Shabbat every prisoner called up to the Torah announced that he was donating years of his life to save her life.
According to Jewishmag, Dov Tamari, who later became a professor at the Technion, donated all his days.
According to Jewishmag, a few days later the daughter's health returned completely, contrary to the medical prognosis.
According to the museum, on the eve of the execution of Moshe Barazani and Meir Feinstein, Yehoshua Zetler, Lehi commander in Jerusalem, came to Reb Aryeh's home and asked his opinion of the plan.
According to the museum, the rabbi was in emotional turmoil, but explicitly opposed the plan for Moshe and Meir to take their own lives.
On the evening before the execution, Rabbi Yaakov Goldman visited them in their cell and decided to accompany them.
Reb Aryeh attended their funeral on the Mount of Olives, although he opposed their act.
According to the museum, he spoke in Acre prison with Dov Gruner and with the three men sentenced over the Night of the Floggings, a day before they were sent to the gallows.
According to Wiki Yeshiva, the military rabbinate was unable to identify with certainty 12 bodies of the men of the Lamed-Heh platoon, and the decision was made by the Gra's lottery.
According to the museum, at the request of the families, Reb Aryeh conducted the lottery in his home in Mishkenot Yisrael.

stations.title: "An old Jew in Jerusalem who loved you"

paragraphs.text: According to Jewishmag, in 1965, for his 80th birthday, veteran underground fighters honored him at a ceremony in the courtyard of the Central Prison.
According to Jewishmag, at the ceremony he asked those present to tell their children that there had been an old Jew in Jerusalem who loved them very much, and burst into tears.

Ten years earlier, in April 1955, according to JTA, the rabbi was presented with a scroll in his honor, signed by some 1,000 former prisoners of the British from the Mandate days, at a reunion of the former prisoners held in the former Central Prison.
According to his grandson, there was a special bond between him and Menachem Begin.
According to the grandson, he also conducted the wedding of Yitzhak Shamir, later Lehi commander and prime minister.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, he refused all honors, including the Freedom of Jerusalem, and never moved out of the poor Mishkenot neighborhood.

stations.title: The farewell, and the house that remained

paragraphs.text: Reb Aryeh died in 1969.
According to the Lehi website, he was buried in Sanhedria, beside his wife.
According to Wiki Yeshiva, he asked in his will that no eulogies be given for him.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, tens of thousands, including prominent figures, attended his funeral.
After his death, the street on which he lived was named after him, and the government medals company issued a medal in his memory.
The Museum of Underground Prisoners in Jerusalem operates under the Ministry of Defense.

claims.quote: מפני שהיה נוהג במשך כעשרים וחמש שנה, כבר בתקופת המנדט הבריטי, ללכת לאסירים בבתי הכלא

claims.text: לפי JTA, כ-1,000 אסירים לשעבר של הבריטים חתמו על מגילה לכבוד הרב באירוע התייחדות בכלא לשעבר.
claims.quote: he was presented with a scroll, signed by some 1,000 former prisoners of the British during the Mandate days, paying tribute to him

claims.text: לפי הביוגרפיה של המוזיאון, בעקבות פנייה לרבנות הראשית הרב קוק המליץ על ר' אריה, והוא הסכים לתפקיד בתנאי שלא יקבל שכר.
claims.quote: המליץ הרב הראשי קוק על ר' אריה. כאשר הבריטים ביקשו את הסכמתו הוא נאות לקבל את התפקיד ובתנאי שלא יקבל שכר

claims.text: לפי הביוגרפיה של המוזיאון, ר' אריה שוחח בבית הכלא בעכו עם דב גרונר ושלושת נידוני ליל ההלקאות יום לפני העלאתם לגרדום.
